claim: In Huntington's disease, a mutated version of the huntingtin protein leads to cell death.
source: In Huntington's disease, a mutated version of the huntingtin protein leads to cell death.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about Huntington's disease stated in the abstract, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Mutant huntingtin is known to aggregate.
source: Mutant huntingtin is known to aggregate, a process that can be inhibited by the eukaryotic chaperonin TRiC (TCP1-ring complex) in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Mutant huntingtin aggregation can be inhibited by the eukaryotic chaperonin TRiC in vitro and in vivo.
source: Mutant huntingtin is known to aggregate, a process that can be inhibited by the eukaryotic chaperonin TRiC (TCP1-ring complex) in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: TRiC caps mhttQ51 fibril tips via the apical domains of its subunits.
source: We find that TRiC caps mhttQ51 fibril tips via the apical domains of its subunits, and also encapsulates smaller mhtt oligomers within its chamber.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from cryo-EM and tomography.

claim: TRiC encapsulates smaller mhtt oligomers within its chamber.
source: We find that TRiC caps mhttQ51 fibril tips via the apical domains of its subunits, and also encapsulates smaller mhtt oligomers within its chamber.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from cryo-EM and tomography.

claim: The two complementary mechanisms of fibril capping and oligomer encapsulation provide a structural description for TRiC's inhibition of mhttQ51 aggregation in vitro.
source: These two complementary mechanisms provide a structural description for TRiC's inhibition of mhttQ51 aggregation in vitro.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: The presence of huntingtin aggregates in the brain correlates strongly with functional deficits in individuals with Huntington's disease.
source: The presence of huntingtin aggregates in the brain correlates strongly with functional deficits in individuals with Huntington's disease (HD) (DiFiglia et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to DiFiglia et al., 1997.

claim: A mutation in the huntingtin gene causes an expansion of glutamine repeats in the huntingtin protein.
source: These aggregates originate from a mutation in the huntingtin gene that causes an expansion of glutamine (Q) repeats in the huntingtin protein (Zoghbi and Orr, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zoghbi and Orr, 2009.

claim: Polyglutamine expansion greater than 36 residues contributes to mutant huntingtin's tendency to aggregate within the cell.
source: This polyglutamine expansion (Q>36) contributes to mutant huntingtin's (mhtt) tendency to aggregate within the cell (Nekooki-Machida et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nekooki-Machida et al., 2009.

claim: TRiC is a key regulator of protein aggregation.
source: Some chaperones, such as the eukaryotic chaperonin TRiC, are key regulators of protein aggregation (Muchowski and Wacker, 2005; Liebman and Meredith, 2010; Voisine et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Muchowski and Wacker, 2005; Liebman and Meredith, 2010; Voisine et al., 2010.

claim: TRiC modulates and suppresses polyglutamine aggregation, including that of mhtt variants having polyQ tracts of different length.
source: In fact, TRiC modulates and suppresses polyglutamine aggregation, including that of mhtt variants having polyQ tracts of different length.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: TRiC's inhibition of mhtt aggregation has been biochemically characterized for several variants both in vitro and in vivo.
source: TRiCs inhibition of mhtt aggregation has been biochemically characterized for several variants both in vitro and in vivo (Kitamura et al., 2006; Tam et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kitamura et al., 2006; Tam et al., 2006.

claim: TRiC is a ∼1 MDa double-ring complex.
source: TRiC is a ∼1 MDa double-ring complex that interacts with ∼10% of all cytosolic proteins and is stringently required for the proper folding of many essential proteins (Yam et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a structural characteristic of TRiC supported by citation.

claim: TRiC interacts with approximately 10% of all cytosolic proteins.
source: TRiC is a ∼1 MDa double-ring complex that interacts with ∼10% of all cytosolic proteins and is stringently required for the proper folding of many essential proteins (Yam et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yam et al., 2008.

claim: TRiC is stringently required for the proper folding of many essential proteins.
source: TRiC is a ∼1 MDa double-ring complex that interacts with ∼10% of all cytosolic proteins and is stringently required for the proper folding of many essential proteins (Yam et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yam et al., 2008.

claim: TRiC can assume different conformations in different biochemical states.
source: TRiC can assume different conformations in different biochemical states (Cong et al., 2012) and can bind substrates like actin and tubulin through different sites, either at its apical tips, which are conformationally flexible in the apo state (Llorca et al., 1999), or inside the chamber (Dekker et al., 2011; Muñoz et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cong et al., 2012.

claim: TRiC can bind substrates like actin and tubulin through different sites, either at its apical tips or inside the chamber.
source: TRiC can assume different conformations in different biochemical states (Cong et al., 2012) and can bind substrates like actin and tubulin through different sites, either at its apical tips, which are conformationally flexible in the apo state (Llorca et al., 1999), or inside the chamber (Dekker et al., 2011; Muñoz et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Llorca et al., 1999; Dekker et al., 2011; Muñoz et al., 2011.

claim: TRiC's apical tips are conformationally flexible in the apo state.
source: TRiC can assume different conformations in different biochemical states (Cong et al., 2012) and can bind substrates like actin and tubulin through different sites, either at its apical tips, which are conformationally flexible in the apo state (Llorca et al., 1999), or inside the chamber (Dekker et al., 2011; Muñoz et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Llorca et al., 1999.

claim: TRiC's interactions with polyQ aggregates are likely to be variable.
source: TRiC's interactions with polyQ aggregates are also likely to be variable, as seen with other chaperone/substrate complexes (Kim et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on analogy to other chaperone/substrate complexes, supported by citation.

claim: There is no existing structural model for how TRiC suppresses mhtt aggregation.
source: There is no existing structural model for how TRiC suppresses mhtt aggregation, and most structural biology techniques are not suited to characterize conformationally heterogeneous specimens such as mhtt aggregates in complex with TRiC.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: Most structural biology techniques are not suited to characterize conformationally heterogeneous specimens such as mhtt aggregates in complex with TRiC.
source: There is no existing structural model for how TRiC suppresses mhtt aggregation, and most structural biology techniques are not suited to characterize conformationally heterogeneous specimens such as mhtt aggregates in complex with TRiC.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of structural biology techniques, based on established knowledge.

claim: Cryo-electron microscopy can preserve specimens in close-to-solution conformations because the samples remain frozen-hydrated without chemical fixation or staining during the entire microscopy session.
source: However, cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) can preserve specimens in close-to-solution conformations because the samples remain frozen-hydrated without chemical fixation or staining during the entire microscopy session (Dubochet et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dubochet et al., 1988.

claim: Cryo-electron tomography allows for visualization of entire protein aggregates in 3-D.
source: Additionally, cryo-electron tomography (cryoET) allows for visualization of entire protein aggregates in 3-D.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of cryoET, based on established knowledge.

claim: Single particle tomography (SPT) has facilitated the determination of the structure of heterogeneous specimens by classifying and averaging subvolumes containing a 3-D view of individual macromolecular complexes.
source: Furthermore, 3-D subtomogram processing approaches (Walz et al., 1997; Böhm et al., 2000; Bartesaghi et al., 2008; Förster et al., 2008; Schmid and Booth, 2008), also known as single particle tomography (SPT), have facilitated the determination of the structure of heterogeneous specimens by classifying and averaging subvolumes containing a 3-D view of individual macromolecular complexes, potentially with different conformations and compositions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Walz et al., 1997; Böhm et al., 2000; Bartesaghi et al., 2008; Förster et al., 2008; Schmid and Booth, 2008.

claim: SPT is an emerging technique in structural biology that can resolve the structure of heterogeneous macromolecular complexes at nanometer resolution.
source: Indeed, SPT is an emerging technique in structural biology that can resolve the structure of heterogeneous macromolecular complexes at nanometer resolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of SPT, based on established knowledge.

claim: At 45 min post-initiation of aggregation in the absence of TRiC, a few isolated mhttQ51 fibrils are visible.
source: At 45 min post-initiation of aggregation (PIA) in the absence of TRiC, we see a few isolated mhttQ51 fibrils (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the 2-D cryoEM images shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Even at early time points, mhttQ51 fibers exhibit extensive heterogeneity, varying both in length and width.
source: Even at early time points, mhttQ51 fibers exhibit extensive heterogeneity, varying both in length and width, with the tips appearing more tapered than the bulk of the fiber.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The tips of mhttQ51 fibers appear more tapered than the bulk of the fiber.
source: Even at early time points, mhttQ51 fibers exhibit extensive heterogeneity, varying both in length and width, with the tips appearing more tapered than the bulk of the fiber.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Thin mhttQ51 fibrils progress to form thicker fibers and eventually form branched-out aggregates or 'sheaves' with a dense central core by 4 hr PIA.
source: By a process that is not yet fully understood, thin fibrils progress to form thicker fibers, and eventually form branched-out aggregates or 'sheaves' with a dense central core by 4 hr PIA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the 2-D cryoEM images shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The process by which thin mhttQ51 fibrils progress to form thicker fibers is not yet fully understood.
source: By a process that is not yet fully understood, thin fibrils progress to form thicker fibers, and eventually form branched-out aggregates or 'sheaves' with a dense central core by 4 hr PIA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: At longer incubation times, there is a dramatic increase in the number and thickness of mhttQ51 sheaves.
source: At longer incubation times, we observe a dramatic increase in the number and thickness of such sheaves, characterized as large fiber bundles densely packed in their central regions and splayed out at both ends.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The number of mhttQ51 sheaves and their thickness appears to plateau at 24 hr PIA.
source: The number of sheaves and their thickness appears to plateau at 24 hr PIA (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the 2-D cryoEM images shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In the presence of TRiC, not even thin mhttQ51 fibrils are visible at 45 min PIA.
source: On the other hand, in the presence of TRiC, not even thin mhttQ51 fibrils are visible at early time points (45 min PIA; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an observation from the 2-D cryoEM images shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At 4 hr and 24 hr PIA in the presence of TRiC, sparse fibrils and a few small sheaves are present, but there are no aggregates as large as those seen in the absence of TRiC at the same time points.
source: At 4 hr and 24 hr PIA (Figure 1E,F), sparse fibrils and a few small sheaves are present, but there are no aggregates as large as those seen in the absence of TRiC at the same time points (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is an observation from the 2-D cryoEM images shown in Figures 1E, 1F, 1B, and 1C.

claim: TRiC does not completely decorate mhttQ51 fibrils, but rather binds at discrete locations, which are often discernible fibril tips.
source: TRiC does not completely decorate mhttQ51 fibrils, but rather binds at discrete locations, which are often discernible fibril tips (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: This is an observation from the 2-D cryoEM images shown in Figures 1G and 1H.

claim: In a 2-D cryoEM image, the entire volume of the actual specimen is projected onto a plane.
source: In a 2-D cryoEM image, the entire volume of the actual specimen is projected onto a plane; therefore, some TRiCs seemingly close to a fibril in 2-D might be floating above or below it and not bound at all.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of 2-D cryoEM imaging, based on established knowledge.

claim: Some TRiCs seemingly close to a fibril in 2-D might be floating above or below it and not bound at all.
source: In a 2-D cryoEM image, the entire volume of the actual specimen is projected onto a plane; therefore, some TRiCs seemingly close to a fibril in 2-D might be floating above or below it and not bound at all.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of 2-D cryoEM imaging.

claim: 2-D cryoEM images cannot unambiguously show whether TRiC is directly bound to mhttQ51.
source: Since 2-D cryoEM images cannot unambiguously show whether TRiC is directly bound to mhttQ5, we performed cryoET experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of 2-D cryoEM imaging.

claim: 3-D tomograms show that TRiC does not fully decorate mhtt fibrils, but rather seems to bind at discrete locations, which often are discernible fibril tips.
source: As in our 2-D images, our 3-D tomograms also show that TRiC does not fully decorate mhtt fibrils, but rather seems to bind at discrete locations, which often are discernible fibril tips.
evidence: This is an observation from the 3-D tomograms.

claim: Visual estimates from 3-D tomograms indicate that 37% (120 of 326) of fibril-bound TRiCs locate to obvious and clearly discernible tips.
source: Our visual estimates from these 3-D tomograms indicate that 37% (120 of 326) of fibril-bound TRiCs locate to obvious and clearly discernible tips.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the 3-D tomograms.

claim: About half of the distinguishable fibril tips seem clearly capped by TRiC.
source: Conversely, about half of the distinguishable fibril tips seem clearly capped by TRiC, but many tips (capped or uncapped) might be obscured by the dense tangles, or may exist as short stubs budding from the side of thicker fibers, which might not be discernible.
evidence: This is an observation from the 3-D tomograms.

claim: Many fibril tips (capped or uncapped) might be obscured by the dense tangles, or may exist as short stubs budding from the side of thicker fibers, which might not be discernible.
source: Conversely, about half of the distinguishable fibril tips seem clearly capped by TRiC, but many tips (capped or uncapped) might be obscured by the dense tangles, or may exist as short stubs budding from the side of thicker fibers, which might not be discernible.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential limitations in the observations.

claim: Given the low signal to noise ratio of individual tomograms, their inherently anisotropic resolution, and 'missing wedge' distortions, it is challenging to visually discern all TRiC molecules and mhtt fibril tips that might be present in crowded fibrillar tangles.
source: In fact, given the low signal to noise ratio (S/N) of individual tomograms, their inherently anisotropic resolution, and 'missing wedge' distortions present in all cryoET data, it is challenging to visually discern all TRiC molecules and mhtt fibril tips that might be present in our crowded fibrillar tangles.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the cryoET technique.

claim: Some fibril-bound TRiCs might be bound to fibril tips barely 'budding out' from the sides of fibril bundles, too short to be discerned.
source: In addition, some fibril-bound TRiCs might be bound to fibril tips barely 'budding out' from the sides of fibril bundles, too short to be discerned.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential limitations in the observations.

claim: The number of TRiCs that locate to tips is likely to be underestimated when counting only those that are on visually discernible tips.
source: Therefore, the number of TRiCs that locate to tips is likely to be underestimated when counting only those that are on visually discernible tips.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of the observations.

claim: Two distinct populations of particles similar in size and shape to TRiC were identified in both 2-D images and 3-D tomograms.
source: In both our 2-D images (Figure 1G–H) and 3-D tomograms (Figure 2, Video 1), we identified two distinct populations of particles similar in size and shape to TRiC.
evidence: This is an observation from the 2-D images and 3-D tomograms.

claim: Particles in one population seem to be attached to mhttQ51 fibrils ('fibril-bound TRiC'), while those in the other do not ('freestanding TRiC').
source: Particles in one population seem to be attached to mhttQ51 fibrils ('fibril-bound TRiC'), while those in the other do not ('freestanding TRiC').
evidence: This is an observation from the 2-D images and 3-D tomograms.

claim: A total of 326 fibril-bound TRiC subvolumes were extracted from tomograms and processed using a completely bias-free subvolume alignment and averaging strategy.
source: We processed a total of 326 fibril-bound TRiC subvolumes extracted from our tomograms using a completely bias-free subvolume alignment and averaging strategy ('Materials and methods' under 'Single particle tomography [SPT]').
evidence: This is a description of the data processing methodology.

claim: 326 fibril-bound TRiC subvolumes represented about one quarter of 1216 TRiC subvolumes extracted from all mhtt-TRiC tomograms combined.
source: This represented about one quarter of 1216 TRiC subvolumes extracted from all our mhtt-TRiC tomograms combined.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the data.

claim: The heterogeneity of fibril-bound TRiC sets precluded them from converging to a single structure and thwarted the determination of specific binding sites between TRiC and mhttQ51 fibrils.
source: Although the heterogeneity of our fibril-bound TRiC sets precluded them from converging to a single structure and thwarted the determination of specific binding sites between TRiC and mhttQ51 fibrils, all our datasets yielded consistent barrel-shaped averages clearly resembling TRiC, with extra mass at the ends of the barrel.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the data analysis.

claim: All fibril-bound TRiC datasets yielded consistent barrel-shaped averages clearly resembling TRiC, with extra mass at the ends of the barrel.
source: Although the heterogeneity of our fibril-bound TRiC sets precluded them from converging to a single structure and thwarted the determination of specific binding sites between TRiC and mhttQ51 fibrils, all our datasets yielded consistent barrel-shaped averages clearly resembling TRiC, with extra mass at the ends of the barrel.
evidence: This is an observation from the SPT analysis.

claim: The extra densities in fibril-bound TRiC averages are attributable to conformational averages of heterogeneous mhttQ51 fibrils.
source: These extra densities are attributable to conformational averages of heterogeneous mhttQ51 fibrils.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SPT analysis results.

claim: A few fibril-bound TRiC averages suggest a mode in which the fibrils might bind predominantly to the tip of a single CCT subunit, while others show mass splayed across the ring, making additional contacts.
source: A few averages suggest a mode in which the fibrils might bind predominantly to the tip of a single CCT subunit, while others show mass splayed across the ring, making additional contacts.
evidence: This is an observation from the SPT analysis of fibril-bound TRiC.

claim: A total of 890 freestanding TRiC subvolumes were extracted from tomograms and processed using SPT.
source: We extracted a total of 890 freestanding TRiC subvolumes from our tomograms and performed SPT (i.e., subvolume alignment, classification, and averaging).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing methodology.

claim: 890 freestanding TRiC subvolumes were about three quarters of the 1216 TRiC subvolumes extracted from all mhtt-TRiC tomograms combined.
source: These were about three quarters of the 1216 TRiC subvolumes extracted from all our mhtt-TRiC tomograms combined.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the data.

claim: When processing the freestanding TRiC subvolumes from each tomogram separately, SPT averages were consistent with the results from the combined data set.
source: When processing the subvolumes from each tomogram separately, SPT averages were consistent with the results from the combined data set, indicating a high level of self-consistency in the results.
evidence: This is a statement about the consistency of the data analysis results.

claim: Statistical analyses suggest that freestanding TRiC subvolumes can be divided into two statistically separable populations.
source: Our statistical analyses ('Materials and methods' under 'Criteria to discriminate between cavity-empty and cavity-occupied freestanding TRIC', Figure 4) suggest that, while the freestanding TRiC subvolumes exhibit a high but continuous level of variability (Figure 4A), they can be divided into two statistically separable populations (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The two statistically separable populations of freestanding TRiC appear to correspond to cavity-empty and cavity-occupied TRiC.
source: These populations appear to correspond to cavity-empty and cavity-occupied TRiC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical analysis results.

claim: The final cavity-empty TRiC average from the combined dataset highly resembles apo-TRiC.
source: The final cavity-empty TRiC average from the combined dataset highly resembles apo-TRiC and was produced using the same bias-free approach applied to fibril-bound TRiC ('Materials and methods' under 'Single particle tomography [SPT]').
evidence: This is an observation from the SPT analysis.

claim: The cavity-empty TRiC average is pseudo eightfold symmetrical, barrel-shaped, and hollow.
source: The average is pseudo eightfold symmetrical, barrel-shaped, and hollow (Figure 5A), and accounts for almost one third of the entire 1216 TRiC subvolumes extracted from all of our mhtt-TRiC tomograms combined.
evidence: This is an observation from the SPT analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The cavity-empty TRiC average accounts for almost one third of the entire 1216 TRiC subvolumes extracted from all mhtt-TRiC tomograms combined.
source: The average is pseudo eightfold symmetrical, barrel-shaped, and hollow (Figure 5A), and accounts for almost one third of the entire 1216 TRiC subvolumes extracted from all of our mhtt-TRiC tomograms combined.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the data.

claim: The cavity-occupied TRiC average has significant extra density lining the interior of the chaperonin's cavity, attributable to a poorly localized substrate.
source: Applying the same bias-free approach to the cavity-occupied TRiC set (also about one third of the entire 1216 TRiC subvolumes) produced an average with significant extra density lining the interior of the chaperonin's cavity, attributable to a poorly localized substrate (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an observation from the SPT analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The cavity-occupied TRiC set represents about one third of the entire 1216 TRiC subvolumes.
source: Applying the same bias-free approach to the cavity-occupied TRiC set (also about one third of the entire 1216 TRiC subvolumes) produced an average with significant extra density lining the interior of the chaperonin's cavity, attributable to a poorly localized substrate (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the data.

claim: When TRiC in the absence of mhtt was processed identically to TRiC in the presence of mhtt, no subset with significant extra density inside the cavity could be identified.
source: When this data was processed identically, we could not identify any subset with significant extra density inside the cavity.
evidence: This is an observation from the control experiment.

claim: The large encapsulated density seen in mhtt-TRiC data derives from the incubation of TRiC with mhtt, rather than residual substrate remaining from the TRiC purification process.
source: This strongly suggests that the large encapsulated density seen in our mhtt-TRiC data derives from the incubation of TRiC with mhtt, rather than residual substrate remaining from the TRiC purification process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the control experiment results.

claim: The Fourier shell correlation (FSC) between the cavity-empty and cavity-occupied TRiC averages gives a value of approximately 52 Å using the FSC = 0.333 threshold.
source: Computing the Fourier shell correlation (FSC) between the cavity-empty and cavity-occupied TRiC averages gives a value of ∼52 Å using the FSC = 0.333 threshold.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of the resolution of the maps.

claim: Comparing the cavity-empty and cavity-occupied TRiC maps to the published apo-TRiC structure using the FSC = 0.5 cutoff yields values of approximately 48 Å and approximately 46 Å respectively.
source: Comparing the maps to the published apo-TRiC structure (Cong et al., 2012) using the FSC = 0.5 cutoff ('Materials and methods' under 'Assessment of the quality of bias-free freestanding TRiC averages'; Figure 7), yields similar values, ∼48 Å and ∼46 Å for cavity-occupied and cavity-empty TRiC respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of the resolution of the maps shown in Figure 7.

claim: A hollow-template-guided alignment strategy was adopted to further localize the interior density in the cavity-occupied TRiC data set.
source: To further localize the interior density in the cavity-occupied TRiC data set, we adopted a hollow-template-guided alignment strategy ('Materials and methods' under 'Localization of density within cavity-occupied TRiC SPT average').
evidence: This is a description of the data processing methodology.

claim: The hollow-template-guided analysis results in a TRiC average with a large density asymmetrically located within the cavity.
source: This additional analysis results in a TRiC average with a large density asymmetrically located within the cavity (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is an observation from the hollow-template-guided analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The interior mass in the cavity-occupied TRiC average is clearly seen in a difference map between the cavity-empty and the cavity-occupied averages.
source: The interior mass is clearly seen in a difference map between the cavity-empty and the cavity-occupied averages (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is an observation from the difference map shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The template used in the hollow-template-guided analysis was completely hollow, and therefore model bias cannot account for the extra density inside.
source: Of note, the template was completely hollow, and therefore model bias cannot account for the extra density we see inside.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology to rule out model bias.

claim: The TRiC part of the cavity-occupied average is pseudo eightfold symmetric.
source: The TRiC part of this cavity-occupied average is also pseudo eightfold symmetric (Figure 8A) and the dip in the rotational correlation plot (or 'u-shaped' path of the overall curves) can be explained by the presence of internal mass, localized to one side of the cavity when viewed end-on ('Materials and methods' under 'Localization of density within cavity-occupied TRiC SPT average', 'Estimation of the size of mhttQ51 oligomers encapsulated by TRiC').
evidence: This is an observation from the hollow-template-guided analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The dip in the rotational correlation plot for the cavity-occupied average can be explained by the presence of internal mass, localized to one side of the cavity when viewed end-on.
source: The TRiC part of this cavity-occupied average is also pseudo eightfold symmetric (Figure 8A) and the dip in the rotational correlation plot (or 'u-shaped' path of the overall curves) can be explained by the presence of internal mass, localized to one side of the cavity when viewed end-on ('Materials and methods' under 'Localization of density within cavity-occupied TRiC SPT average', 'Estimation of the size of mhttQ51 oligomers encapsulated by TRiC').
evidence: This is an interpretation of the rotational correlation plot.

claim: The aggregation and suppression of aggregation reactions followed well characterized conditions, previously described using filter trap assays that detect mhttQ51 amyloid aggregates.
source: Our aggregation and suppression of aggregation reactions followed well characterized conditions, previously described using filter trap assays that detect mhttQ51 amyloid aggregates (Tam et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental methodology, supported by citation.

claim: The mhtt concentration in the experiments was chosen to allow mhtt aggregation to occur in a reasonably short time in the absence of TRiC.
source: The mhtt concentration in our experiments was chosen to allow mhtt aggregation to occur in a reasonably short time in the absence of TRiC (Scherzinger et al., 1999), and the ratio of TRiC to mhtt was chosen to yield initial-stage fibril aggregates and yet thwart large-aggregate growth (Behrends et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design, supported by citation.

claim: The ratio of TRiC to mhtt was chosen to yield initial-stage fibril aggregates and yet thwart large-aggregate growth.
source: The mhtt concentration in our experiments was chosen to allow mhtt aggregation to occur in a reasonably short time in the absence of TRiC (Scherzinger et al., 1999), and the ratio of TRiC to mhtt was chosen to yield initial-stage fibril aggregates and yet thwart large-aggregate growth (Behrends et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design, supported by citation.

claim: The TRiC:mhtt ratio under normal physiological conditions has not been carefully explored.
source: It is worth noting however that the TRiC:mhtt ratio under normal physiological conditions has not been carefully explored.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Increasing cellular levels of TRiC has a beneficial effect in suppressing mhtt toxicity and aggregation.
source: Nonetheless, increasing cellular levels of TRiC has a beneficial effect in suppressing mhtt toxicity and aggregation (Behrends et al., 2006; Kitamura et al., 2006; Tam et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Behrends et al., 2006; Kitamura et al., 2006; Tam et al., 2006.

claim: The formation of groups of sheaves as seen in Figure 1C could correspond to the large inclusions observed in cells expressing mhtt.
source: In our 2-D cryoEM images, the formation of groups of sheaves as seen in Figure 1C could correspond to the large inclusions observed in cells expressing mhtt.
evidence: This is a speculation about the biological relevance of the observations.

claim: The smaller aggregates observed in the presence of TRiC could correspond to the multiple, smaller foci seen in cells overexpressing TRiC or some of its subunits.
source: On the other hand, the smaller aggregates (Figures 1E,F and 3), which are not detectable by filter-trap assays, could correspond to the multiple, smaller foci seen in cells overexpressing TRiC or some of its subunits (Behrends et al., 2006; Tam et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculation about the biological relevance of the observations, supported by citation.

claim: Overexpression of TRiC is known to suppress mhtt toxicity in a variety of systems.
source: Importantly, overexpression of TRiC is known to suppress mhtt toxicity in a variety of systems (Behrends et al., 2006; Kitamura et al., 2006; Tam et al., 2006) and thus our observations provide a structural basis for the observed effect of TRiC.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Behrends et al., 2006; Kitamura et al., 2006; Tam et al., 2006.

claim: The observations provide a structural basis for the observed effect of TRiC in suppressing mhtt toxicity.
source: Importantly, overexpression of TRiC is known to suppress mhtt toxicity in a variety of systems (Behrends et al., 2006; Kitamura et al., 2006; Tam et al., 2006) and thus our observations provide a structural basis for the observed effect of TRiC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in the context of previous work.

claim: After the nucleation stage, small and thin irregular fibrils with exposed hydrophobic moieties ('fibril tips') drive the growth of the aggregates into large sheaves.
source: We envision the progression of mhttQ51 aggregation as a process whereby, after the nucleation stage, small and thin irregular fibrils with exposed hydrophobic moieties ('fibril tips') drive the growth of the aggregates into large sheaves.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observations.

claim: TRiC is known to bind hydrophobic motifs via its apical substrate-binding domains.
source: TRiC is known to bind hydrophobic motifs via its apical substrate-binding domains (Spiess et al., 2006), and has also been shown to crosslink with the N-terminal N17 motif of mhtt, which drives mhtt oligomerization (Tam et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Spiess et al., 2006.

claim: TRiC has been shown to crosslink with the N-terminal N17 motif of mhtt, which drives mhtt oligomerization.
source: TRiC is known to bind hydrophobic motifs via its apical substrate-binding domains (Spiess et al., 2006), and has also been shown to crosslink with the N-terminal N17 motif of mhtt, which drives mhtt oligomerization (Tam et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tam et al., 2009.

claim: The binding between mhttQ51 fibrils and TRiC may involve mhttQ51 hydrophobic moieties that include the N17 domain.
source: It is therefore likely that the binding we demonstrate here between mhttQ51 fibrils and TRiC (Figures 1–3), which thwarts the progression of fibers into sheaves, may involve mhttQ51 hydrophobic moieties that include the N17 domain.
evidence: This is a speculation based on previous knowledge and the current observations.

claim: The N17 domain has been proposed to function as a 'molecular switch' controlled by multiple post-translational modifications that can determine the fate of mhtt exon-1.
source: Interestingly, this domain has been proposed to function as a 'molecular switch' (Greiner and Yang, 2011) controlled by multiple post-translational modifications that can determine the fate of mhtt exon-1 either by rendering it innocuous or enhancing its pathogenicity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Greiner and Yang, 2011.

claim: By virtue of its interaction with the N17 domain, TRiC might provide a protective effect against deleterious post-translational modifications.
source: By virtue of its interaction with the N17 domain, TRiC might provide a protective effect against deleterious post-translational modifications.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential mechanism of TRiC's protective effect.

claim: The fibril-capping mechanism could explain why inhibition of aggregation is observed in vitro at substoichiometric ratios of TRiC to mhtt.
source: This fibril-capping mechanism could explain why inhibition of aggregation is observed in vitro at substoichiometric ratios of TRiC to mhtt.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the fibril-capping mechanism.

claim: The fibril-capping mechanism may explain why mhtt aggregates look different in vivo when TRiC is overexpressed, and become SDS soluble.
source: It may also explain why mhtt aggregates look different in vivo when TRiC is overexpressed, and become SDS soluble (Tam et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the fibril-capping mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: TRiC might bind fibrils through one of its ends while the binding sites at the other end remain available to snatch mhttQ51 oligomers lurking in their proximity.
source: It is conceivable that TRiC might bind fibrils through one of its ends while the binding sites at the other end remain available to snatch mhttQ51 oligomers lurking in their proximity.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential mechanism.

claim: Internalization of smaller mhttQ51 oligomers would contribute to inhibition of sheaf formation by decreasing the effective concentration of oligomers in the reaction mixture.
source: On the other hand, internalization of smaller mhttQ51 oligomers would also contribute to inhibition of sheaf formation by decreasing the effective concentration of oligomers in the reaction mixture.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of inhibition.

claim: Other substrates have been shown to bind deep inside the cavity of apo-TRiC.
source: Although other substrates have also been shown to bind deep inside the cavity of apo-TRiC (Muñoz et al., 2011), the finding that mhtt exon-1 might also be encapsulated is unprecedented.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Muñoz et al., 2011.

claim: The finding that mhtt exon-1 might be encapsulated by TRiC is unprecedented.
source: Although other substrates have also been shown to bind deep inside the cavity of apo-TRiC (Muñoz et al., 2011), the finding that mhtt exon-1 might also be encapsulated is unprecedented.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding.

claim: Extra density is only detectable in approximately 10% of the TRiC particles in the absence of added mhtt.
source: For instance, our controls show that extra density is only detectable in ∼10% of the particles in the absence of added mhtt.
evidence: This is an observation from the control experiment.

claim: Significant extra density is seen in approximately 40-50% of the freestanding TRiC particles from TRiC + mhtt tomograms.
source: On the other hand, we see significant extra density in ∼40–50% of the freestanding TRiC particles from our TRiC + mhtt tomograms.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated that TRiC does not bind GST.
source: Furthermore, previous studies have demonstrated that TRiC does not bind GST (Feldman et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Feldman et al., 2003.

claim: It is unlikely that either native substrates or the GST moiety that is cleaved from mhttQ51 to initiate aggregation could account for the internalized mass observed.
source: Therefore, it is unlikely that either native substrates or the GST moiety that is cleaved from mhttQ51 to initiate aggregation could account for the internalized mass we observe (Figures 5B and 8).
evidence: This is an inference based on the control experiments and previous knowledge.

claim: The internalized density likely represents mhtt.
source: Rather, this density likely represents mhtt.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and controls.

claim: Estimates suggest an average size of approximately 60 kDa for the encapsulated mass.
source: However, our estimates suggest an average size of ∼60 kDa ('Materials and methods' under 'Estimation of the size of mhttQ51 oligomers encapsulated by TRiC'), which would correspond to an oligomer of about six mhttQ51 exon1 monomers.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate based on the data analysis.

claim: An encapsulated mass of approximately 60 kDa would correspond to an oligomer of about six mhttQ51 exon1 monomers.
source: However, our estimates suggest an average size of ∼60 kDa ('Materials and methods' under 'Estimation of the size of mhttQ51 oligomers encapsulated by TRiC'), which would correspond to an oligomer of about six mhttQ51 exon1 monomers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mass estimate.

claim: The mhttQ51 oligomers that might be encapsulated by TRiC could be analogous to precursor forms of the 100–230 kDa toxic oligomers previously reported.
source: The mhttQ51 oligomers that might be encapsulated by TRiC could be analogous to precursor forms of the 100–230 kDa toxic oligomers previously reported (Behrends et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculation about the nature of the encapsulated oligomers, supported by citation.

claim: It is possible that the extra density inside TRiC corresponds to an average of encapsulated mhtt oligomers of different sizes and conformations.
source: Furthermore, it is possible that the extra density we see inside TRiC (Figures 5B and 8) corresponds to an average of encapsulated mhtt oligomers of different sizes and conformations.
evidence: This is a speculation about the heterogeneity of the encapsulated oligomers.

claim: The compositional and conformational heterogeneity of the specimen precludes resolving nanometer resolution structures from it with any technique in structural biology other than SPT.
source: The compositional and conformational heterogeneity of such a specimen precludes resolving nanometer resolution structures from it with any technique in structural biology other than SPT.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of structural biology techniques and the advantages of SPT.

claim: The approach demonstrates TRiC's association with mhttQ51 fibrillar aggregates.
source: Indeed, our approach demonstrates TRiC's association with mhttQ51 fibrillar aggregates, and our results suggest TRiC might also sequester small mhttQ51 oligomers to effectively inhibit mhtt aggregation (Figure 9, Video 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The results suggest TRiC might sequester small mhttQ51 oligomers to effectively inhibit mhtt aggregation.
source: Indeed, our approach demonstrates TRiC's association with mhttQ51 fibrillar aggregates, and our results suggest TRiC might also sequester small mhttQ51 oligomers to effectively inhibit mhtt aggregation (Figure 9, Video 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: This novel mechanism contrasts with those typically proposed for the action of chaperones in suppressing aggregation of misfolded proteins by binding monomeric forms.
source: This novel mechanism contrasts with those typically proposed for the action of chaperones in suppressing aggregation of misfolded proteins (Hendrick and Hartl, 1995; Young et al., 2004) by binding monomeric forms.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: The analysis lacks the sensitivity to distinguish TRiCs that might be bound to one mhtt monomer only.
source: However, since our analysis lacks the sensitivity to distinguish TRiCs that might be bound to one mhtt monomer only, we cannot rule out that such a binding mode may co-exist with the ones presented here.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the analysis.

claim: It cannot be ruled out that TRiC binding to monomeric mhtt may co-exist with the fibril-capping and oligomer-encapsulation mechanisms.
source: However, since our analysis lacks the sensitivity to distinguish TRiCs that might be bound to one mhtt monomer only, we cannot rule out that such a binding mode may co-exist with the ones presented here.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: The observation that TRiC can bind substrates via its apical domains is consistent with the current understanding of TRiC–substrate interactions.
source: While our observation that TRiC can bind substrates via its apical domains is consistent with the current understanding of TRiC–substrate interactions, our data is unprecedented in demonstrating the direct binding of fibrils (a substrate too large to be internalized).
evidence: This is a statement about the consistency of the findings with previous knowledge.

claim: The data is unprecedented in demonstrating the direct binding of fibrils (a substrate too large to be internalized) by TRiC.
source: While our observation that TRiC can bind substrates via its apical domains is consistent with the current understanding of TRiC–substrate interactions, our data is unprecedented in demonstrating the direct binding of fibrils (a substrate too large to be internalized).
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding.

claim: The suggestion that TRiC might cap fibril growth as well as internalize smaller oligomers indicates a broad scope for this chaperonin's action on protein aggregates.
source: The suggestion that TRiC might cap fibril growth as well as internalize smaller oligomers indicates a broad scope for this chaperonin's action on protein aggregates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The ability of TRiC to recognize and handle both oligomers and fibrillar aggregates could account for the reduced toxicity of mhtQ51 and other mhtt species when TRiC is overexpressed in cells.
source: The ability of TRiC to recognize and handle both types of proposed mhtt toxic species observed in Huntington's disease (DiFiglia et al., 1997; Arrasate and Finkbeiner, 2011; Nucifora et al., 2012), namely oligomers and fibrillar aggregates, could account for the reduced toxicity of mhtQ51 and other mhtt species when TRiC is overexpressed in cells (Behrends et al., 2006; Tam et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: Oligomers and fibrillar aggregates are the two types of proposed mhtt toxic species observed in Huntington's disease.
source: The ability of TRiC to recognize and handle both types of proposed mhtt toxic species observed in Huntington's disease (DiFiglia et al., 1997; Arrasate and Finkbeiner, 2011; Nucifora et al., 2012), namely oligomers and fibrillar aggregates, could account for the reduced toxicity of mhtQ51 and other mhtt species when TRiC is overexpressed in cells (Behrends et al., 2006; Tam et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to DiFiglia et al., 1997; Arrasate and Finkbeiner, 2011; Nucifora et al., 2012.

claim: TRiC's interaction with mhtt aggregates might render them more amenable to processing by cellular pathways of quality control, such as autophagy and proteolytic degradation by the proteasome.
source: TRiC's interaction with mhtt aggregates might render them more amenable to processing by cellular pathways of quality control, such as autophagy and proteolytic degradation by the proteasome (Sarkar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential mechanism of TRiC's protective effect, supported by citation.

claim: Mhtt oligomers and fibrillar aggregates are strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of Huntington's disease.
source: Since mhtt oligomers and fibrillar aggregates are strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of Huntington's disease (Sathasivam et al., 2010), the interactions that we describe between TRiC and mhttQ51 provide a structural mechanism for the chaperonin's aggressive inhibition of mhtt aggregation in vitro and suggest a potential for TRiC-inspired therapeutics (Sontag et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sathasivam et al., 2010.

claim: The interactions described between TRiC and mhttQ51 provide a structural mechanism for the chaperonin's aggressive inhibition of mhtt aggregation in vitro.
source: Since mhtt oligomers and fibrillar aggregates are strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of Huntington's disease (Sathasivam et al., 2010), the interactions that we describe between TRiC and mhttQ51 provide a structural mechanism for the chaperonin's aggressive inhibition of mhtt aggregation in vitro and suggest a potential for TRiC-inspired therapeutics (Sontag et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The interactions described between TRiC and mhttQ51 suggest a potential for TRiC-inspired therapeutics.
source: Since mhtt oligomers and fibrillar aggregates are strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of Huntington's disease (Sathasivam et al., 2010), the interactions that we describe between TRiC and mhttQ51 provide a structural mechanism for the chaperonin's aggressive inhibition of mhtt aggregation in vitro and suggest a potential for TRiC-inspired therapeutics (Sontag et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation about the therapeutic implications of the findings, supported by citation.

claim: Aggregation of GST-mhttQ51 at a concentration of 6 µM was initiated in vitro by adding AcTEV protease.
source: Aggregation of GST-huntingtin exon 1 fusion proteins with 51 glutamine repeats (GST-mhttQ51) at a concentration of 6 µM was initiated in vitro by adding AcTEV protease (Invitrogen), both alone and in presence of 1.2 µM TRiC at a t = 0 hr (Tam et al., 2006) in TEV Buffer (Invitrogen, Grand Island, NY).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology.

claim: 20 tilt series of mhttQ51 + TRiC at t = 4 hr were collected using SerialEM on a JEM2100 electron microscope.
source: We collected 20 tilt series of mhttQ51 + TRiC at t = 4 hr using SerialEM (Mastronarde, 2005) on a JEM2100 electron microscope equipped with a LaB6 gun operating at 200 kV, from −60° to 60°, at 2° increments, target underfocus of 5 μm, sampling of 4.4 Å/pixel and a cumulative dose of ∼62 e/Å2.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology.

claim: 6 of the 20 tilt series appeared appropriate for tomographic reconstruction and were reconstructed into tomograms using IMOD.
source: 6 of the 20 tilt series appeared appropriate for tomographic reconstruction and were reconstructed into tomograms using IMOD (Kremer et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing methodology.

claim: All SPT processing and averaging was done with subtomograms extracted from the original raw tomograms using e2spt_boxer.py in EMAN2.
source: All SPT processing and averaging was done with subtomograms extracted from the original raw tomograms (unbinned) using e2spt_boxer.py in EMAN2 (Tang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing methodology.

claim: Cross-correlation map normalization was used to avoid missing wedge bias.
source: To avoid missing wedge bias, we used cross-correlation map normalization (Schmid and Booth, 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing methodology, supported by citation.

claim: The bias-free subtomogram processing uses unsupervised hierarchical ascendant classification and averaging (HAC).
source: Our bias-free subtomogram processing uses unsupervised hierarchical ascendant classification and averaging (HAC), a technique involving pairwise alignment of sub-tomograms and clustering based on similarity (Bartesaghi et al., 2008; Förster et al., 2008; Schmid and Booth, 2008), without the aid of a reference and without imposing symmetry at any point.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing methodology, supported by citations.
